algorithm.definition: A precise, step-by-step recipe for solving a problem.

api.definition: Application Programming Interface: a defined way for one program to ask another for data or actions, like a menu in a restaurant.

api-key.definition: A secret code that identifies your program to an API. Treat it like a password: never put it in your code or in Git.

assignment.definition: Pointing a name at a value with =. 'x = 5' means 'x now points to 5'.

backend.definition: The part of an app that runs on a server: it stores data and answers requests. Users never see it directly.

big-o.definition: A way to describe how the work a piece of code does grows as its input grows, e.g. O(n) or O(n²).

binary.definition: Counting with only two digits, 0 and 1. Computers store everything this way.

bit.definition: The smallest piece of data: a single 0 or 1.

boolean.definition: A value that is either True or False. Named after mathematician George Boole.

branch.definition: In Git, a separate line of work, so you can try changes without touching the main version.

breakpoint.definition: A marker that tells the debugger to pause the program at that line so you can inspect it.

bug.definition: When code does something different from what you intended.

byte.definition: 8 bits together. One byte can store a number from 0 to 255.

call-stack.definition: The pile of function calls that are currently running or waiting. The newest call sits on top.

class.definition: A blueprint for creating objects. It defines what data they hold and what they can do.

client.definition: The program that sends a request, like your browser asking a server for a page.

commit.definition: A saved snapshot of your project in Git, with a message describing the change.

conditional.definition: Code that only runs if something is true, written with if / elif / else.

cpu.definition: Central Processing Unit: the chip that follows a program's instructions, billions of times per second.

css.definition: Cascading Style Sheets: the language that sets how a web page looks, like colors, sizes and layout.

data-structure.definition: A way of organizing many values, like a list, dict, set or tuple.

data-type.definition: The kind of a value (whole number, decimal, text, True/False), which decides what you can do with it.

database.definition: A program that stores data safely and lets you search it quickly, even with millions of records.

debugging.definition: Finding out why code doesn't do what you expected, and fixing it.

deployment.definition: Putting your app on a server on the internet so other people can use it.

dns.definition: Domain Name System: the internet's phone book, turning names like example.com into IP addresses.

environment-variable.definition: A named setting your shell gives to programs, like HOME or PATH. Often used for secrets too.

exception.definition: An error that happens while a program runs. It can be 'caught' and handled with try / except.

framework.definition: A ready-made structure for building a type of app. You fill in your own code, and it handles the rest.

frontend.definition: The part of an app users see and interact with, usually running in the browser.

function.definition: A named, reusable block of code that can take inputs and return a result.

garbage-collection.definition: Python automatically freeing memory that no variable points to anymore.

git.definition: The most popular version control tool. It records the history of your code as commits.

html.definition:
HyperText Markup Language: describes the structure and content of a web page, using tags like

and

.

http.definition: HyperText Transfer Protocol: the request-and-response rules browsers and servers use to talk.

ide.definition: Integrated Development Environment: a code editor with extra tools like a debugger and a terminal built in.

indentation.definition: Spaces at the start of a line. In Python, indentation decides which lines belong inside a block.

inheritance.definition: Making a new class based on an existing one, so it gets the existing class's attributes and methods.

interpreter.definition: A program that reads code and runs it step by step. 'python3' is Python's interpreter.

io.definition: Input/Output: data going into or out of a program, such as reading files, typing, or printing.

ip-address.definition: A number that identifies a computer on a network, like 93.184.215.14.

iteration.definition: One trip around a loop. 'Iterating' over a list means going through its items one by one.

javascript.definition: The programming language that runs in web browsers. It makes pages interactive.

json.definition: JavaScript Object Notation: a text format for data that looks like Python dicts and lists.

key-value.definition: A key (like a word) linked to a value (like its definition). Dictionaries store these.

loop.definition: Code that repeats. A 'for' loop goes through items; a 'while' loop repeats while a condition is true.

markdown.definition: A simple way to format plain text: # for headings, ** for bold, - for lists. Used for READMEs.

memory-address.definition: The number that identifies one spot in the computer's memory, like a house number.

method.definition: A function that belongs to an object, called with a dot: name.upper().

module.definition: A Python file whose code you can use in another file with import.

mutable.definition: Can be changed after it's created. Lists and dicts are mutable; strings and tuples are not (immutable).

nodejs.definition: A program that runs JavaScript outside the browser. DevPath's build tools run on it.

object.definition: A value in memory that has a type, data and methods. In Python, everything is an object.

oop.definition: Organizing code into objects that bundle data together with the functions that use it.

operating-system.definition: The main program that manages the computer and runs other programs, e.g. macOS, Windows or Linux.

package.definition: Reusable code published for others to install, e.g. with pip (Python) or npm (JavaScript).

parameter.definition: A named input in a function definition. The actual value passed in is called the argument.

path.definition: The address of a file or folder, like /Users/you/Desktop/notes.txt.

path-variable.definition: An environment variable listing the folders your shell searches when you type a command.

port.definition: A number that picks which program on a computer you're talking to, like localhost:5173.

portfolio.definition: A collection of your best projects that shows employers what you can build.

prompt.definition: The text in the terminal (ending in % or $) that means it's waiting for your command.

protocol.definition: An agreed set of rules for how two programs talk to each other.

pull-request.definition: On GitHub, a request to merge your branch's changes, where others can review them first.

ram.definition: Random Access Memory: the computer's fast, short-term memory for programs that are running. It's cleared when the power goes off.

recursion.definition: When a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of it.

remote.definition: In Git, a copy of your repository stored somewhere else, usually on GitHub. Often named 'origin'.

repository.definition: A project folder tracked by Git, including its whole history. 'Repo' for short.

scope.definition: Where in the code a name can be seen. Variables made inside a function are only visible inside it.

server.definition: A computer or program that waits for requests and sends back responses.

shell.definition: The program inside the terminal that reads and runs your commands. macOS uses zsh.

sql.definition: Structured Query Language: the language for asking databases questions and changing their data.

standard-library.definition: The modules that come built into Python, like math, random and json. No installing needed.

terminal.definition: A window where you type text commands to your computer instead of clicking.

test.definition: A small piece of code that checks other code works as expected.

traceback.definition: Python's error report: what went wrong (last line) and the chain of calls that led there.

url.definition: Uniform Resource Locator: a web address, like https://example.com/about.

variable.definition: A name that points to a value, so your program can use it later.

version-control.definition: A system that records changes to files over time, so you can see history and go back.

virtual-environment.definition: A private folder of Python packages for one project, so projects don't clash.

working-directory.definition: The folder your terminal (or program) is currently 'in'. Relative paths start from here.

localstorage.definition: A small storage area every website gets in your browser. DevPath saves your progress there.

typescript.definition: JavaScript plus types. It catches mistakes before the code runs. DevPath is written in it.

react.definition: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of small, reusable components.
